lessons.title: Context: Romanticism, Science & the Gothic
lessons.description: Romanticism, the Enlightenment, and the Gothic tradition behind Frankenstein.
lessons.content_html:
Mary Shelley and the Birth of Frankenstein

Mary Shelley began writing Frankenstein in the summer of 1816, when she was just eighteen years old. She was staying at Lake Geneva with her future husband, the poet Percy Bysshe Shelley, and their friend Lord Byron. A wet, stormy summer kept the group indoors, and Byron proposed a ghost-story competition. Out of that challenge came one of the most influential novels in English literature. Shelley published Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus anonymously in 1818 — many readers initially assumed a man had written it.

Shelley’s life was shaped by loss. Her mother, the feminist writer Mary Wollstonecraft, died eleven days after giving birth to her. Shelley’s own first child died in infancy. These experiences of birth, death, and the fragility of life permeate the novel. Victor Frankenstein’s attempt to create life — and the catastrophic consequences — reflects Shelley’s deeply personal understanding that the line between creation and destruction is dangerously thin.

Key Fact

Shelley’s three biographical links: (1) her mother died days after childbirth, giving Shelley a lifelong awareness of how creation and death are intertwined; (2) her own infant daughter died, intensifying her sensitivity to loss; (3) she was surrounded by radical thinkers (Percy Shelley, Byron, her father William Godwin) who debated science, religion, and the boundaries of human knowledge.

The Enlightenment and Scientific Progress

The late 18th and early 19th centuries were a period of rapid scientific discovery. The Enlightenment championed human reason as the path to understanding the natural world. Scientists like Luigi Galvani experimented with galvanism — using electricity to stimulate dead tissue — raising the question of whether science could conquer death itself.

Shelley was fascinated by these debates. In her 1831 preface, she described conversations between Percy Shelley and Byron about “the nature of the principle of life” and whether a corpse could be “re-animated.” Victor Frankenstein embodies the Enlightenment scientist pushed to dangerous extremes: he believes that reason and knowledge can overcome all limits, including death. Shelley’s novel asks a profoundly modern question: just because science can do something, does that mean it should?

The novel’s subtitle — The Modern Prometheus — references the Greek myth of Prometheus, who stole fire from the gods and gave it to humanity. Zeus punished Prometheus with eternal torment. Shelley draws a direct parallel: Victor steals the “secret of life” from nature and is punished with the destruction of everything he loves. The myth warns against overreaching — crossing boundaries that were not meant to be crossed. Victor, like Prometheus, brings forbidden knowledge into the world and suffers catastrophically for it.

Romanticism and the Sublime

Romanticism was the dominant literary movement when Shelley wrote Frankenstein. Romantic writers like Wordsworth, Coleridge, Byron, and Percy Shelley celebrated nature, emotion, and the power of the imagination. They also explored the concept of the sublime — the overwhelming awe and terror inspired by nature’s power. Shelley uses sublime landscapes throughout the novel: the Alpine mountains, the Arctic ice, and violent storms.

These landscapes serve as a counterpoint to Victor’s scientific ambition. Nature is vast, beautiful, and utterly indifferent to human plans. Victor repeatedly seeks solace in the Alps after his creations cause disaster, but nature does not provide easy comfort — it reminds him of his own insignificance. Shelley suggests that Victor’s fatal flaw is his refusal to accept natural limits: he tries to conquer death, control creation, and master nature, and nature punishes him for his arrogance.

Key Fact

Shelley uses Romanticism in three key ways: (1) sublime landscapes (Alps, Arctic) represent forces beyond human control; (2) the Creature’s emotional sensitivity and love of nature align him with Romantic ideals more than Victor does; (3) Victor’s scientific rationalism is presented as dangerous precisely because it ignores emotion, empathy, and natural limits — the qualities Romanticism valued most.

The Gothic Tradition

Frankenstein is also a Gothic novel. Gothic fiction features dark settings, the supernatural, extreme emotions, transgression, and the blurring of boundaries between life and death. Shelley uses Gothic conventions throughout: the midnight creation scene with its “dull yellow eye” opening, the charnel houses and graveyards where Victor collects body parts, the murders committed in darkness, and the pursuit across desolate Arctic ice.

But Shelley’s Gothic is also intellectual. The real horror in Frankenstein is not the Creature’s appearance but Victor’s moral failure. He creates a being with human consciousness and then abandons it. The Gothic terror comes from the recognition that the true monster might not be the Creature but the creator who refuses to take responsibility for what he has made.

Frankenstein is often called the first science fiction novel. Unlike earlier Gothic works that relied on supernatural explanations (ghosts, curses), Shelley grounds her horror in science: Victor uses galvanism and anatomy to create life. The novel imagines the consequences of a plausible (for the time) scientific breakthrough, making it a forerunner of modern science fiction’s “what if?” approach. Shelley anticipated debates about genetic engineering, artificial intelligence, and bioethics that are still urgent today.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For AO3, always link context to Shelley’s purpose. Instead of “Galvanism was popular in the early 19th century,” write “Shelley uses Victor’s galvanic experiments to warn against the Enlightenment belief that science can overcome all limits, reflecting contemporary anxieties about rapid scientific progress.” Context should always explain WHY Shelley makes the choices she does.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Shelley wrote Frankenstein at 18, drawing on personal experience of loss (her mother’s death, her infant’s death) and the scientific debates of her circle (galvanism, the “principle of life”).
  • The subtitle “The Modern Prometheus” frames Victor’s story as one of overreaching: stealing forbidden knowledge and suffering catastrophic punishment.
  • The novel blends Gothic horror, Romantic landscapes, and Enlightenment science to ask a question that remains urgent: just because we can, should we?

lessons.title: Walton's Frame & Victor's Ambition
lessons.description: Walton’s frame narrative, Victor’s childhood, and the seeds of dangerous ambition.
lessons.content_html:
Walton’s Frame Narrative

The novel opens with Captain Robert Walton, an explorer writing letters to his sister from a voyage to the North Pole. Walton’s burning desire for glory mirrors Victor’s: both men sacrifice human connection for knowledge. Shelley uses this nested narrative to ensure no single narrator controls the truth. Walton hero-worships Victor, Victor blames the Creature, and the Creature seeks sympathy. The reader must evaluate all three.

Walton writes: “I shall satiate my ardent curiosity with the sight of a part of the world never before visited.” The language of hunger (“satiate”) and passion (“ardent”) echoes Victor’s obsessive pursuit. Both men have no close friends. Shelley structures the novel so Victor’s story serves as a warning to Walton — and to the reader: unchecked ambition destroys the ambitious.

Key Fact

The three-layered narrative (Walton → Victor → Creature) means no account is objective. Each narrator is biased. Shelley uses this structure to challenge assumptions about who is trustworthy and who is the “monster.” The frame also creates a parallel: Walton’s ambition mirrors Victor’s, warning that the destructive pattern could repeat.

Victor’s Childhood and Education

Victor grows up in Geneva in a loving, privileged family. His parents are devoted, Henry Clerval is loyal, and Elizabeth is gentle. Shelley presents his childhood as idyllic to make his later failures more damning — unlike the Creature, Victor has every advantage and still makes catastrophic choices.

As a teenager, Victor obsesses over alchemists like Agrippa and Paracelsus who pursued eternal life. At Ingolstadt, Professor Waldman introduces him to chemistry, igniting his fatal ambition to “penetrate into the recesses of nature and show how she works in her hiding-places.”

During his studies, Victor isolates himself completely. He stops writing to his family, neglects his health, and works in secret. He describes his laboratory as a “workshop of filthy creation” — the adjective “filthy” reveals his subconscious disgust. Shelley shows isolation as both cause and symptom of moral failure. Victor cuts himself off from those who might have restrained him and plunges deeper into obsession.

Victor’s Fatal Decision

Victor discovers “the cause of generation and life” — Shelley never explains what this secret is, focusing attention on moral consequences. Victor declares: “A new species would bless me as its creator and source… No father could claim the gratitude of his child so completely as I should deserve theirs.”

This reveals his true motivation: not scientific progress but personal glory. He wants worship. The language of paternity (“father,” “child,” “gratitude”) becomes bitterly ironic when he immediately abandons his creation. Shelley’s hubris warning: creation without responsibility is cruelty.

Key Fact

Victor’s ambition is selfish: he wants a “new species” to “bless me as its creator.” He assumes he can control what he creates. The Creature’s rebellion proves him catastrophically wrong. Shelley’s central message: ambition without moral responsibility leads to destruction for creator and creation alike.

Walton is Victor’s mirror. Both sacrifice relationships for discovery. Both use the language of conquest about nature. But Walton has a chance Victor never took: he can listen to the warning and turn back. At the novel’s end, Walton’s crew demand they return south — and Walton agrees, abandoning the expedition. He is the one man in the novel who heeds the warning in time, which is why Shelley gives him the last word. Whether humanity at large will learn from its mistakes is the question he leaves with the reader.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When analysing Victor’s ambition, focus on Shelley’s language of power and possession. Words like “bless me,” “creator,” “source” reveal his desire for godlike control. For AO3, link to the Enlightenment and the Prometheus myth. Always explain that Shelley warns against ambition without moral responsibility.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The nested narrative (Walton → Victor → Creature) creates unreliable narration, forcing readers to judge who is credible and who is the real “monster.”
  • Victor’s ambition is selfish: he wants worship, not progress. His paternity language becomes ironic when he abandons the Creature.
  • Walton mirrors Victor, warning that the destructive cycle of unchecked ambition could repeat endlessly.

lessons.title: Creation & Abandonment
lessons.description: The creation scene, Victor’s abandonment, and the horror of irresponsible creation.
lessons.content_html:
The Creation Scene

The creation of the Creature in Chapter 5 is the novel’s most iconic scene. Victor describes the moment: “I saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open; it breathed hard, and a convulsive motion agitated its limbs.” The language is clinical and detached — “it,” not “he” — immediately dehumanising the being Victor has spent years creating. The “dull yellow eye” is the only physical detail Shelley provides of the moment of animation, focusing on a single unsettling image rather than the grand triumph Victor expected.

Victor’s reaction is immediate and total rejection: “breathless horror and disgust filled my heart.” He had imagined creating something beautiful: “His limbs were in proportion, and I had selected his features as beautiful.” But the result horrifies him. Shelley uses this gap between expectation and reality to critique Victor’s hubris. He planned creation like an artist but had no plan for what came after. The moment the Creature lives, Victor’s responsibility begins — and he immediately runs away.

Key Fact

Victor abandons the Creature within moments of its creation. He describes “breathless horror and disgust” and flees to his bedroom. This is the novel’s original sin: a creator who refuses to care for his creation. Shelley parallels this with irresponsible parenthood — the Creature is essentially a newborn, abandoned without language, understanding, or love. Every tragedy that follows stems from this moment of rejection.

The Creature as Newborn

Shelley presents the Creature at its creation as a tabula rasa — a blank slate. It has no language, no knowledge of good or evil, and no understanding of why it exists. When it reaches out to Victor in the bedroom — “he muttered some inarticulate sounds, while a grin wrinkled his cheeks” — Shelley describes what is essentially a baby’s smile. Victor interprets this as menacing; the reader may see it as desperate affection. This ambiguity is deliberate: Shelley asks whether the Creature is born monstrous or made monstrous by its treatment.

The Rousseau-influenced philosophy is clear: the Creature begins as innocent and becomes violent only after repeated rejection, cruelty, and isolation. Shelley’s argument is that society creates monsters, not nature. If Victor had nurtured his creation, the Creature might have been the “new Adam” it later describes itself as. Instead, it becomes the “fallen angel” — a being corrupted not by its own nature but by the world’s cruelty.

The creation scene is charged with Shelley’s personal experience. Her mother died days after giving birth to her. Her first child died in infancy — she recorded dreaming that she could rub the dead baby back to life by the fire. The creation of the Creature — bringing something dead to life through unnatural means, only to face horror and loss — echoes Shelley’s deepest anxieties about the relationship between birth and death. The novel is, at its heart, about what happens when creation goes wrong.

Victor’s Dream and the Corpse of Elizabeth

After fleeing, Victor falls into a disturbed sleep and has a nightmare that is crucial for exam analysis. He dreams of embracing Elizabeth, but as he kisses her, she transforms into the corpse of his dead mother, “shrouded in a flannel.” This dream links creation, death, sexuality, and guilt in a single horrifying image. Shelley connects Victor’s act of unnatural creation with the destruction of natural relationships — by trying to conquer death, Victor has brought death into the heart of his most intimate bonds.

The dream also foreshadows Elizabeth’s murder on their wedding night. Victor’s creation will destroy the woman he loves, just as the dream predicts. Shelley uses foreshadowing throughout the novel to create a sense of inevitable doom — Victor set a catastrophe in motion at the moment of creation, and nothing can stop it.

Key Fact

Victor’s nightmare: he embraces Elizabeth, she turns into his dead mother’s corpse. This links creation (the Creature), death (the mother), and love (Elizabeth) into a single image of corruption. It foreshadows Elizabeth’s murder and symbolises how Victor’s unnatural act of creation has contaminated all his natural relationships. Birth and death have become horribly intertwined.

The creation scene raises the novel’s central question: who is the real monster? Victor creates a conscious being and then abandons it. The Creature did not ask to be made; it entered the world with no understanding and was immediately rejected by the one person who should have cared for it. Shelley makes the reader complicit in Victor’s judgement — we, too, are inclined to see the Creature as horrifying. But the text consistently asks us to reconsider: is the Creature monstrous because of what it looks like, or has Victor’s abandonment created the monster it becomes?
lessons.exam_tip_html: The creation scene is one of the most likely exam extracts. When analysing it, focus on the dehumanising pronoun “it,” the gap between Victor’s expectations and reality, and the Creature’s infant-like behaviour (“inarticulate sounds,” “grin”). For AO3, link to Rousseau’s ideas about natural innocence and Shelley’s personal experience of birth and death. The best responses will argue that Victor’s abandonment, not the Creature’s appearance, is the true horror.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Victor abandons the Creature moments after creation, dehumanising it with the pronoun “it” — this is the novel’s original sin from which all tragedies flow.
  • The Creature begins as a blank slate (Rousseau’s tabula rasa); Shelley argues that society creates monsters, not nature.
  • Victor’s nightmare (Elizabeth turning into his dead mother’s corpse) links creation, death, and love, foreshadowing the destruction of everything Victor values.

lessons.title: The Creature's Story
lessons.description: The Creature’s story: the De Lacey family, education, rejection, and the birth of rage.
lessons.content_html:
The Creature’s Narrative

Chapters 11–16 give the Creature its own voice — the innermost layer of the nested narrative. The Creature tells Victor how it wandered alone after being abandoned, confused by its senses: “A strange multiplicity of sensations seized me, and I saw, felt, heard, and smelt at the same time.” Shelley presents the Creature as experiencing the world like a newborn — overwhelmed, vulnerable, and without any frame of reference. This is her most powerful argument for the Creature’s essential innocence.

The Creature discovers fire and is burned, learns that humans flee from its appearance, and eventually finds shelter in a hovel attached to the cottage of the De Lacey family. It watches them through a crack in the wall, learning language, emotion, and human relationships. Felix teaches Safie (a Turkish woman) to read using Volney’s Ruins of Empires, and the Creature learns alongside her — absorbing knowledge of human history, injustice, and civilisation.

Key Fact

From the De Laceys, the Creature learns: (1) language — giving it the ability to express its suffering and desire for connection; (2) emotion — it feels joy watching the family’s love and weeps at their hardships; (3) self-awareness — it sees its own reflection and realises it is “hideously deformed.” Education gives the Creature the tools to understand its suffering but not the power to escape it.

The Three Books

The Creature finds three books that shape its understanding: Paradise Lost by Milton, Plutarch’s Lives, and The Sorrows of Young Werther by Goethe. Paradise Lost is the most significant. The Creature reads it as “a true history” and identifies with both Adam and Satan. Like Adam, it was created by a “creator” who should have cared for it. Like Satan, it has been cast out and now burns with rejection and rage. The novel’s title-page epigraph — “Did I request thee, Maker, from my clay to mould me Man?” — is drawn from Milton’s Adam in “Paradise Lost”, setting up the central theme of a creator’s responsibility to his creation.

This allusion is central to the novel. Like Adam, the Creature did not ask to be made. Like Satan, it has been rejected by its creator and now seeks revenge. Shelley asks the reader: if God abandoned Adam, would Adam be justified in turning to evil? The Creature’s identification with both figures creates deep moral ambiguity — it is simultaneously sympathetic (abandoned child) and terrifying (vengeful outcast).

The Creature’s plan is careful and rational. It approaches old De Lacey when the rest of the family is away, knowing the blind man cannot judge it by appearance. The conversation is moving: De Lacey responds with kindness, calling the Creature “friend.” For a brief moment, genuine human connection seems possible. But when Felix, Agatha, and Safie return, they see the Creature and react with horror and violence. Felix beats it with a stick. The family abandons their cottage the next day. The one chance for acceptance is destroyed by visual prejudice.

The Birth of Rage

After the De Lacey rejection, the Creature describes a fundamental shift: “From that moment I declared everlasting war against the species.” The word “everlasting” and the phrase “declared war” mark a transformation from victim to aggressor. Shelley does not excuse the Creature’s subsequent violence, but she makes clear what caused it: systematic, universal rejection based on appearance alone. The Creature tried kindness, reason, and patience. Every attempt was met with horror and violence. Shelley’s argument is disturbing: society’s refusal to see beyond surface appearance creates the very monsters it fears.

The Creature also finds Victor’s journal and learns the full horror of its creation: that Victor was disgusted by it from the moment of its birth. It discovers it was made from dead body parts and that its creator considered it an abomination. This knowledge — that it was never loved, never even tolerated — completes the Creature’s transformation. It heads for Geneva to confront Victor, fuelled by a mixture of grief and rage.

Key Fact

“From that moment I declared everlasting war against the species” marks the Creature’s turning point. It is not born violent — it is made violent by: (1) Victor’s abandonment at creation, (2) universal human rejection based on its appearance, (3) the De Lacey family’s violent response to its attempt at friendship, and (4) discovering Victor’s journal, which reveals it was always considered an abomination. Shelley argues that monstrosity is created by society, not by nature.

The Creature’s story is Shelley’s strongest statement on the nature versus nurture debate. The Creature begins with the capacity for love, compassion, and learning. It weeps at the De Laceys’ suffering, saves a drowning girl, and gathers firewood for the cottage family. Every instinct is generous. It is only after repeated, universal rejection that it turns to violence. Shelley, influenced by Rousseau, argues that humans (and human-like beings) are made good or evil by their treatment, not by their inherent nature. Victor’s failure to nurture his creation is the root cause of all the novel’s tragedies.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The Creature’s narrative is where Shelley’s moral argument is most powerful. When analysing these chapters, always consider the Creature’s perspective sympathetically before discussing its violence. Show that you understand Shelley’s Rousseau-influenced argument about nature vs nurture. The strongest exam responses will argue that the Creature’s violence is a product of Victor’s failure and society’s prejudice, not innate evil.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Creature begins as innocent — it learns language, emotion, and self-awareness from the De Laceys. Its identification with both Adam and Satan from Paradise Lost creates deep moral ambiguity.
  • The De Lacey rejection is the turning point: the one chance for acceptance is destroyed by visual prejudice. The Creature declares “everlasting war against the species.”
  • Shelley’s argument: monstrosity is created by society (abandonment, rejection, prejudice), not by nature. The Creature’s story is a powerful case for nurture over nature.

lessons.title: Murder, Revenge & the Bride
lessons.description: The murders of William and Justine, the destroyed bride, and the cycle of revenge.
lessons.content_html:
The Murder of William

The Creature’s first murder is Victor’s youngest brother, William. The Creature encounters William in the woods near Geneva and initially hopes the child will be unprejudiced: “This little creature was unprejudiced and had lived too short a time to have imbibed a horror of deformity.” But William screams, calls the Creature a “monster” and an “ogre,” and reveals he is a Frankenstein. The Creature kills him in a rage and plants a miniature portrait on the sleeping Justine Moritz to frame her.

Shelley makes this murder morally complex. The Creature’s first instinct is hope, not violence — even now, it craves connection. But William’s reaction (learned prejudice from society) confirms what the Creature already fears: no human will ever accept it. The child’s name, “Frankenstein,” triggers the Creature’s rage because it targets Victor’s family — the one thing Victor values. The murder is the Creature’s first deliberate act of revenge against its creator.

Key Fact

William’s murder shows the Creature has not lost its desire for connection — it approaches the child hoping for acceptance. The murder is triggered by rejection and the name “Frankenstein.” The framing of Justine adds a calculated cruelty: the Creature has learned from human society how to manipulate justice. Shelley shows that the Creature mirrors the cruelty it has received.

Justine’s Trial and Death

Justine Moritz is tried and executed for William’s murder despite being innocent. Victor knows the truth but stays silent, too afraid to reveal the existence of the Creature. Justine’s name is bitterly ironic — “Justine” means “justice,” yet she receives none. Shelley uses her death to criticise both Victor’s cowardice and the legal system that condemns an innocent woman on circumstantial evidence and a coerced confession.

Victor describes his guilt: “The blood of the murdered one was not more terrible to me than the anguish of the living victim of my machinations.” Yet his guilt produces no action — he weeps, he agonises, but he does nothing to save Justine. Shelley presents Victor’s passivity as a moral crime equal to the Creature’s violence. Justine is destroyed by two “monsters”: the Creature who framed her and Victor who could have saved her.

The Creature confronts Victor on the Mer de Glace and demands a female companion: “I am alone and miserable; man will not associate with me; but one as deformed and horrible as myself would not deny herself to me.” The appeal is rational and deeply sympathetic — the Creature does not ask for revenge or power, only for companionship. It promises to leave humanity forever if Victor creates a mate. Victor initially agrees, then destroys the half-finished female in front of the Creature. This second abandonment — the deliberate destruction of hope — triggers the Creature’s most devastating acts of revenge.

The Destruction of the Female Creature

Victor begins creating a female companion in Scotland but stops, horrified by the implications. He fears the two creatures might breed, creating a “race of devils.” He also fears the female might have her own will and reject the male Creature. Victor destroys the half-finished female while the Creature watches from the window. This act of destruction is presented as a point of no return.

The Creature’s response is chilling and devastating: “I shall be with you on your wedding-night.” Victor interprets this as a threat against himself. But the Creature means Elizabeth. Shelley creates dramatic irony: Victor prepares to defend himself on his wedding night, never considering that the Creature will target the person he loves most. The Creature has learned Victor’s logic perfectly: you destroyed my companion, so I will destroy yours.

Key Fact

“I shall be with you on your wedding-night” is the novel’s most important piece of dramatic irony. Victor assumes the threat is against him; the Creature means Elizabeth. By destroying the female, Victor removed the Creature’s only hope. The Creature’s response is a mirror of Victor’s own action: “You destroyed my chance for companionship, so I will destroy yours.” The cycle of creation and destruction repeats.

After the female’s destruction, the Creature murders Henry Clerval — Victor’s closest friend and the character who most represents warmth, loyalty, and human connection. Henry’s death strips Victor of his last source of genuine companionship, mirroring the Creature’s own isolation. Shelley structures each murder to remove the people Victor loves one by one, making him experience the loneliness the Creature has felt since birth. The punishment fits the crime: Victor created a being and denied it love, so the Creature destroys everyone who loves Victor.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about the murders, always analyse both the Creature’s motivation and Victor’s complicity. The Creature’s violence is wrong, but Shelley makes clear that Victor’s abandonment and the destruction of the female companion are the causes. The strongest responses argue that both Victor and the Creature are responsible for the deaths, not just the one who committed them.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • William’s murder shows the Creature still craving connection even as it turns violent — the killing is triggered by rejection and the name “Frankenstein.” Justine’s execution exposes both the Creature’s cruelty and Victor’s cowardice.
  • The Creature’s demand for a female companion is rational and sympathetic, but Victor’s destruction of the half-finished female removes all hope and triggers the deadliest revenge.
  • “I shall be with you on your wedding-night” creates dramatic irony: Victor misinterprets the threat, and the Creature mirrors his cruelty by destroying Victor’s chance for companionship.

lessons.title: The Pursuit & the Ending
lessons.description: Elizabeth’s murder, the Arctic pursuit, and the deaths of Victor and the Creature.
lessons.content_html:
The Murder of Elizabeth

On his wedding night, Victor arms himself and patrols the house, convinced the Creature’s threat was directed at him. He leaves Elizabeth alone in their room. When he hears her scream, he rushes in to find her dead: “She was there, lifeless and inanimate, thrown across the bed, her head hanging down and her pale and distorted features half covered by her hair.” The Gothic imagery — the lifeless body, distorted features, hair covering the face — mirrors the creation scene in reverse: where Victor once brought dead matter to life, the Creature now brings death to the living.

Victor’s failure to protect Elizabeth is a structural echo of his failure to nurture the Creature. In both cases, he is absorbed in his own concerns and fails to see the obvious threat. The Creature watches through the window, “a grin on its face,” paralleling the “grin” it wore at its creation. Shelley closes the circle: the smile the creator rejected has become the smile of the destroyer. Everything the Creature was denied — love, a partner, a wedding night — it now takes from Victor.

Key Fact

Elizabeth’s murder is the creation scene in reverse: Victor once brought dead matter to life; now the Creature brings death to life. The Creature’s grin through the window echoes its newborn smile, turning innocence into menace. Victor’s failure to protect Elizabeth mirrors his failure to nurture the Creature — in both cases, his self-absorption leads to destruction.

The Arctic Pursuit

After Elizabeth’s death and his father’s death from grief, Victor pursues the Creature across Europe and into the Arctic. The pursuit reverses their original roles: Victor, the creator, is now the one chasing; the Creature, once the pursuer of human connection, now flees. The Arctic setting is sublime — vast, desolate, and utterly indifferent to human suffering. Shelley places the final confrontation in the most inhospitable landscape on Earth, symbolising the emotional wasteland both characters now inhabit.

The Creature leaves food for Victor along the trail, keeping him alive so the pursuit can continue. This detail is deeply disturbing: the Creature wants Victor to suffer as long as possible. But it can also be read as the Creature’s last perverse act of connection — Victor is the only being who acknowledges the Creature’s existence. Their relationship, however destructive, is the only relationship either of them has left.

Victor dies aboard Walton’s ship, exhausted by the pursuit. His final words to Walton are telling: even on his deathbed, he cannot decide whether his creation was right or wrong. He warns Walton against ambition but also says: “‘yet another may succeed’.” This ambiguity is deliberate — Shelley refuses to give Victor a neat moral resolution. He dies as he lived: brilliant, tormented, and unable to take full responsibility for what he has done.

The Creature’s Final Speech

The Creature appears over Victor’s dead body and delivers its final speech to Walton. This is one of the most powerful passages in the novel. The Creature mourns Victor: “That is also my victim! In his murder my crimes are consummated.” The word “consummated” (meaning completed or fulfilled) links death to marriage, echoing the wedding-night murder. The Creature is not triumphant — it is devastated. Revenge brought no satisfaction, only emptier isolation.

The Creature declares it will travel to the “most northern extremity of the globe” and build its own funeral pyre: “I shall die. I shall no longer feel the agonies which now consume me.” It leaps from the ship window and is “borne away by the waves and lost in darkness and distance.” Shelley ends the novel with ambiguity: we do not see the Creature die. It vanishes into the sublime Arctic, leaving the reader to wonder whether it truly ends or continues to haunt the edges of the world.

Key Fact

The Creature’s final speech reveals that revenge brought no peace: “In his murder my crimes are consummated” shows recognition that destroying Victor destroyed the Creature’s last connection to another being. The planned funeral pyre represents the Creature’s only remaining choice: self-destruction. Shelley’s message is that the cycle of revenge ultimately annihilates both creator and creation.

The novel ends where it began: with Walton in the Arctic. His crew demand they turn back south. Walton yields to them: he abandons the quest and turns the ship for home, heeding the warning Victor gave but could not follow himself. What Shelley leaves ambiguous is not Walton’s choice but the Creature’s ending. It is borne away into darkness and distance, and we never see it die. The moral question returns to the reader. Will humanity learn from Victor’s mistake? Will ambition be tempered by responsibility? Walton’s retreat suggests the warning can be heard, but the Creature’s unwitnessed fate leaves the novel’s final question open.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When writing about the ending, focus on the Creature’s eloquence and grief. The strongest responses note that the Creature is more articulate and self-aware than Victor in their final moments. Analyse “consummated” (linking death and marriage) and “borne away… in darkness and distance” (ambiguous disappearance). For AO3, discuss the sublime Arctic setting and its connection to Romantic ideas about human insignificance.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Elizabeth’s murder reverses the creation scene: death replaces life, and the Creature’s grin through the window transforms its newborn smile into a destroyer’s triumph.
  • The Arctic pursuit places the final confrontation in a sublime, desolate landscape that symbolises the emotional wasteland both characters inhabit.
  • The Creature’s final speech reveals that revenge brought only deeper suffering. The ambiguous ending — the Creature vanishing into darkness — leaves the moral question unresolved.

lessons.title: Key Themes & Exam Technique
lessons.description: Key themes, essential quotations, and AQA exam technique for Frankenstein essays.
lessons.content_html:
The Five Major Themes

Every essay on Frankenstein connects to one or more key themes. The five most commonly tested are: dangerous knowledge and ambition, creation and responsibility, monstrosity and prejudice, isolation and companionship, and nature versus nurture.

Key Fact

Dangerous Knowledge: "So much has been done — far more will I achieve" (Victor's Promethean ambition). Creation & Responsibility: "A new species would bless me as its creator" (Victor wants worship, not responsibility). Monstrosity: "I saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open" (the pronoun 'it' dehumanises from birth). Isolation: "I am alone and miserable" (the Creature's plea for a companion). Nature vs Nurture: "From that moment I declared everlasting war against the species" (society creates the monster).

Key Quotations Bank

"A new species would bless me as its creator and source." — Victor's hubris: he wants godlike worship.

"Workshop of filthy creation" — "filthy" reveals Victor's subconscious disgust at his own work.

"Breathless horror and disgust filled my heart." — Victor's immediate rejection of his creation.

"Did I request thee, Maker, from my clay to mould me man?" — the novel’s title-page epigraph draws from Paradise Lost, challenging Victor's right to create and abandon.

"I am alone and miserable; man will not associate with me." — The Creature's most sympathetic plea.

"I shall be with you on your wedding-night." — The Creature's threat, creating dramatic irony.

"In his murder my crimes are consummated." — Revenge brings no peace; "consummated" links death and marriage.

"Everywhere I see bliss, from which I alone am irrevocably excluded." — The Creature's awareness of its permanent isolation.

What the 19th-Century Novel Question Tests

Your response is assessed on three strands: your critical response to the text with well-chosen references (AO1), your analysis of the writer's methods — language, structure and form (AO2), and your understanding of context (AO3). You will receive a printed extract (~400 words) and must write about the extract AND the novel as a whole. Check your exam board's specimen paper and mark scheme for the exact weightings and timings that apply to your exam.

Key Fact

AO1 — Critical response: Build a clear argument supported by well-chosen references from the extract AND the whole novel. AO2 — Writer's methods: Analyse Shelley's methods — language, structure, narrative voice, symbolism. AO3 — Context: Embed context (Enlightenment, Romanticism, Gothic, biography). Never bolt context on as a separate paragraph.

Essay Structure

Use PEALCE: Point → Evidence → Analyse Language → Link to Context → Evaluate. Balance extract analysis (2–3 paragraphs) with whole-novel references (2–3 paragraphs). The biggest mark differentiator is close analysis of methods — analyse what they do, don't just identify them.

Point: Shelley presents Victor's rejection of the Creature as an act of parental failure. Evidence: "I saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open; it breathed hard." Analysis: The pronoun "it" immediately dehumanises the Creature, denying it personhood. The focus on a single "dull yellow eye" reduces the being to one unsettling detail, reflecting Victor's inability to see beyond surface appearance. The passive phrasing — "it breathed" rather than "he breathed" — distances Victor from responsibility. Context: Shelley, whose own mother died in childbirth, was deeply aware that creation carries moral obligations. Victor's rejection of a conscious being echoes the Enlightenment's blind faith in progress without consideration of consequences. Evaluate: This moment establishes Shelley's central argument: the true horror is not the Creature's appearance but the creator's refusal to take responsibility.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The highest marks go to responses that analyse Shelley’s methods, not just themes. Instead of “Shelley shows science is dangerous,” write “Shelley’s use of the dehumanising pronoun ‘it’ reveals Victor’s instant denial of the Creature’s personhood, critiquing the Enlightenment’s pursuit of knowledge without moral responsibility.” Always explain the effect of specific words on the reader.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Prepare quotations for five themes: dangerous knowledge, creation/responsibility, monstrosity/prejudice, isolation/companionship, nature vs nurture. 2–3 quotations per theme.
  • The 30-mark question needs balanced extract + whole-novel analysis. Embed context; never bolt it on.
  • Use PEALCE. Focus on AO2: analyse Shelley’s language choices and their effects on the reader.
